beats.say: Your Wi-Fi works a lot like a walkie-talkie. Your router broadcasts radio, and every device nearby is listening.
When you open a page, your request becomes radio waves, flies to the router, and the answer comes back the same way.
Here's the catch. All of those devices share one channel, and in general only one can talk at a time.
So they take turns, in tiny slices of time, so quick that you never notice the gaps.
Add more devices, and the line gets longer. Everyone waits a little more, so everything feels slower.
Wi-Fi comes in two main bands. The lower one, two point four gigahertz, travels further and passes through walls better.
The higher one, five gigahertz, is usually faster, but its signal fades quickly, especially through walls.
So if your Wi-Fi crawls, move closer to the router, or switch your device to the five gigahertz band.
That's why a quiet house feels fast, and a crowded one does not.
